CHAPTER 5 · LEARNING AREA 5 · APRIL · MAY

Maths in everyday life

How many handshakes are there in a class? Is the dice loaded? Is the big pack really cheaper? In this chapter you learn strategies for cracking problems, carry out random experiments and evaluate them, and you talk precisely about connections: if – then and the more – the more.

15 LESSONS3 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • try systematically, work backwards and reduce a problem to something familiar
  • carry out random experiments, count with tally charts and give absolute and relative frequencies
  • use if – then and the more – the more correctly and check them with counterexamples
  • plan a short presentation on packaging
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

What percentage is $\tfrac{3}{4}$?

$\tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{75}{100} = 75\%$

12 out of 20 as a decimal?

$\tfrac{12}{20} = \tfrac{6}{10} = 0.6$

5 exercise books cost €4. What do 10 exercise books cost?

twice as many, twice as expensive: €8

UNIT 15 LESSONS

1Problem-solving strategies

There are chickens and rabbits in a hutch. Together they have 8 heads and 22 legs. How many rabbits are there? You do not have a formula for this yet – but you can try cleverly.

Good problem solvers carry a few tools in their heads. Trying systematically means: in order, in a table, forgetting nothing, nothing twice. When working backwards, you start at the result and undo every step.

If a problem is too big, you reduce it to something familiar: start smaller, look for a pattern, split it into sub-problems. A sketch almost always helps.

KEY POINT · FOUR STRATEGIES

Sketch and table: make the problem visible

Trying systematically: in order, note down every attempt

Working backwards: start from the result, with the inverse operation: $+$ becomes $-$, $\cdot$ becomes $:$

Reducing to something familiar: start smaller, look for patterns, solve sub-problems · and always: check!

Four steps: understand the problem, make a plan, carry out the plan, look back – that is how George Pólya described it in 1945 in “How to Solve It”.

Backwards: first it was doubled, then 7 was added? Then first subtract 7, then halve.

INTERACTIVE · WORKING BACKWARDS

On the right is the result of the chain of calculations. Work back step by step and type in the starting number. The chain calculates forwards as a check.

EXAMPLE 1 · TRYING WITH A TABLE

8 heads, 22 legs. How many rabbits and how many chickens?

Rabbits 0 → 16 legs, 1 → 18, 2 → 20, 3 → 22 ✓. Each rabbit brings 2 more legs.

3 rabbits and 5 chickens – check: $3 \cdot 4 + 5 \cdot 2 = 22$ ✓

EXAMPLE 2 · WORKING BACKWARDS

Lea thinks of a number, doubles it, adds 7 and gets 31. Which number did she think of?

Backwards: $31 - 7 = 24$, $24 : 2 = 12$.

12 – check: $2 \cdot 12 + 7 = 31$ ✓

EXERCISES

I think of a number, multiply it by 3, subtract 5 and get 40. Which number is it?

$40 + 5 = 45$, $45 : 3 = 15$. Check: $3 \cdot 15 - 5 = 40$ ✓

Tom spends half his money on a book, then €4 on an ice cream. Now he has €6 left. How much did he have at the start?

Backwards: $6 + 4 = 10$, $10 \cdot 2 = 20$. He had €20.

Each person shakes hands with every other person once. How many handshakes are there with 5 people? And with 25?

Start smaller: 2 → 1, 3 → 3, 4 → 6, 5 → 10 (pattern +2, +3, +4). With 25 people each shakes 24 hands, and then every handshake is counted twice: $25 \cdot 24 : 2 = 300$.

Two numbers have the sum 30 and the difference 8. What are they?

Trying: 15 and 15 (difference 0), 17 and 13 (4), 19 and 11 (8) ✓. The numbers are 19 and 11.

How many squares (of all sizes) can you find on a grid of 4 × 4 small squares?

Split by size: 16 small, 9 of 2 × 2, 4 of 3 × 3, 1 large: $16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 30$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Times 3, minus 5, gives 40: which number?

$(40 + 5) : 3 = 15$

Handshakes with 6 people?

$6 \cdot 5 : 2 = 15$

10 heads and 28 legs: how many rabbits?

All chickens: 20 legs. Each rabbit 2 more: $(28 - 20) : 2 = 4$

UNIT 25 LESSONS

2Random experiments and frequencies

When you roll a dice, nobody knows beforehand which number will come up. The only certain thing is: it will be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. An experiment like this is called a random experiment. What comes out of it is the outcome.

If you repeat the experiment often, you count with a tally chart. How often an outcome occurred is its absolute frequency. If you divide by the number of trials, you get the relative frequency – as a fraction, as a decimal or as a percentage.

Each outcome is assigned its frequency. That is an assignment: you can show it as a table or as a bar chart.

KEY POINT · FREQUENCIES

absolute frequency: how often an outcome occurred

relative frequency $= \dfrac{\text{absolute frequency}}{\text{number of trials}}$

All the relative frequencies together add up to $1 = 100\%$.

Tally chart: every fifth stroke is drawn across. That way you count quickly in bundles of five.

The more trials, the closer the relative frequency usually comes to the chance, for a dice $\tfrac{1}{6}$.

INTERACTIVE · COIN, DICE, SPINNER

Choose an experiment and run it 10 or 100 times. The table shows absolute and relative frequencies, the dashed line the chance.

EXAMPLE 3 · RELATIVE FREQUENCY

In 50 rolls the 6 came up exactly 9 times. Give the relative frequency.

$\tfrac{9}{50} = \tfrac{18}{100} = 0.18$

18% – a little more than $\tfrac{1}{6} \approx 17\%$

EXAMPLE 4 · THE OTHER SIDE

A coin is tossed 40 times, and it comes up heads 22 times. How big is the relative frequency of tails?

Tails came up $40 - 22 = 18$ times: $\tfrac{18}{40} = 0.45$.

45% – together with heads (55%) that makes 100%.

EXERCISES

Which outcomes are possible? a) tossing a coin   b) rolling a dice   c) a spinner with red, blue, green   d) the month of birth of a randomly chosen person

a) heads, tails   b) 1 to 6   c) red, blue, green   d) the 12 months

A dice was rolled 30 times: 1 came up 4 times, 2 came up 6 times, 3 came up 5 times, 4 came up 3 times, 5 came up 7 times, 6 came up 5 times. Give the relative frequencies of 4 and of 5.

4: $\tfrac{3}{30} = 0.1 = 10\%$.   5: $\tfrac{7}{30} \approx 0.23 \approx 23\%$.

In 200 throws, a drawing pin lands on its back 124 times. Give the relative frequency. About how often do you expect “back” in 1000 throws?

$\tfrac{124}{200} = 0.62 = 62\%$. In 1000 throws about 620 times.

In a class, 8 name maths, 10 PE, 4 art and 3 German as their favourite subject. Give all the relative frequencies as percentages.

25 people asked: maths 32%, PE 40%, art 16%, German 12%. Together 100% ✓

Lina has rolled a dice 6 times and not got a 6. She says: “The dice is loaded.” Is she right?

No. 6 rolls are far too few. Six times without a 6 happens in roughly every third attempt. Only after many rolls can you say anything.

TEST YOURSELF!

9 sixes in 50 rolls: relative frequency in %?

$\tfrac{9}{50} = \tfrac{18}{100}$

40 coin tosses, 22 times heads: relative frequency of tails in %?

$\tfrac{18}{40} = 0.45$

124 times on its back in 200 throws: relative frequency as a decimal?

$124 : 200 = 0.62$

UNIT 35 LESSONS

3If – then and the more – the more

“If it rains, then the street is wet.” That is true. But is this also true: “If the street is wet, then it is raining”? No – perhaps only the street-cleaning lorry has been past. A statement and its converse have to be checked separately.

In mathematics, an if-then statement says: if the condition is met, then the conclusion holds. “If a quadrilateral is a square, then it has four right angles.” The converse is false: a rectangle also has four right angles. A single counterexample is enough to disprove a statement.

The-more-the-more statements describe the direction of a connection: “The more exercise books, the higher the price.” “The more people, the smaller the pieces.” But a connection is only proportional if double belongs to double (or to half).

KEY POINT · SPEAKING PRECISELY

If – then: condition → conclusion. Check the converse separately. A counterexample disproves.

The more – the more: for example directly proportional · the more – the less: for example inversely proportional

“The more – the more” on its own does not yet mean proportional.

Presentation: choose a topic (architecture, design, packaging), measure, make a table, state the result with “the more – the more”, design a poster.

Sustainable: less packaging material means less waste. The surface area from chapter 4 is the material.

INTERACTIVE · THE FURTHER, THE MORE EXPENSIVE

For the taxi: the further, the more expensive. Does double the distance cost double? Compare with the apples and the cake.

EXAMPLE 5 · CHECKING THE CONVERSE

“If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even.” Is the statement true? Is its converse true?

The statement is true: $4 = 2 \cdot 2$. Converse: “If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4.” Counterexample: 6.

statement true, converse false

EXAMPLE 6 · PACKAGING

1 litre of juice in one cube with a 10 cm edge or in 8 cubes with a 5 cm edge: how much material do you need?

Large cube: $6 \cdot 100 = 600$ cm². Small cubes: $8 \cdot 6 \cdot 25 = 1200$ cm².

twice as much material – the smaller the packs, the more material for the same amount.

EXERCISES

Complete: a) The faster you drive, the … (same distance)   b) The more litres you fill up with, the …   c) The more people share a pizza, the …

a) shorter the journey time   b) higher the price   c) smaller the pieces

True or false? Check the converse too. a) If a quadrilateral is a square, then all its sides are equal in length.   b) If a number ends in 0, then it is divisible by 5.

a) true; converse false (rhombus).   b) true; converse false (15).

“The older a person, the taller they are.” When is that true, and when not? Is height proportional to age?

It is only roughly true until people stop growing, at around 18. Not proportional: at 10 you are not twice as tall as at 5 (about 140 cm instead of 110 cm).

The longer the edge of a cube, the bigger its volume. Calculate the volume for the edges 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm. Is the volume proportional to the edge?

1 cm³, 8 cm³, 27 cm³. Not proportional: double the edge gives eight times the volume.

1 litre = 1000 cm³ is packed into 1000 little cubes with a 1 cm edge. How much material do you need? Compare with the cube from example 6.

$1000 \cdot 6 = 6000$ cm², ten times as much as the 600 cm² of the large cube.

TEST YOURSELF!

“If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4.” The smallest positive counterexample?

2 is even, but not divisible by 4.

A cube with a 2 cm edge: volume in cm³?

$2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$

8 cubes with a 5 cm edge: total surface area in cm²?

$8 \cdot 150 = 1200$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A water lily doubles its area every day. After 20 days the pond is completely covered. When was it half covered?

Backwards: one day before, on day 19.

A spinner was spun 60 times: red 28 times, blue 21 times, green 11 times. Calculate the relative frequencies as percentages. Does that fit a spinner that is half red, one third blue and one sixth green?

Red ≈ 47%, blue = 35%, green ≈ 18%. The chances are 50%, about 33% and about 17% – that fits well.

Muesli: 500 g cost €2.49, 1 kg costs €3.99. Calculate the price per 100 g for each. Is “the bigger the pack, the cheaper” always true?

500 g: about €0.50 per 100 g. 1 kg: about €0.40 per 100 g. Here it is true – but not always: offers and special prices sometimes turn it round. That is why you compare the unit price.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Ten thousand coin tosses

Does a coin really come up heads in half the cases in the long run? Some researchers wanted to know exactly and tossed very often.

WhoTossesHeadsrelative
Buffon, 177740402048≈ 0.507
Kerrich, 1940–194510,0005067≈ 0.507
Pearson, around 190024,00012,012≈ 0.501

The mathematician John Kerrich was interned in a camp in Jutland during the Second World War. There he tossed a coin 10,000 times and kept an exact record. None of the three got exactly half – but all of them are very close to it. The more tosses, the smaller the deviation from 0.5 usually becomes.

Try it yourself: The class tosses a coin 1000 times altogether. How close do you get to 0.5?

Sources: G.-L. Leclerc de Buffon, “Essai d’arithmétique morale”, 1777; J. E. Kerrich, “An Experimental Introduction to the Theory of Probability”, Copenhagen 1946. Pearson’s figures are quoted in statistics textbooks.

$(23 - 5) : 2 = 9$

$(38 - 24) : 2 = 7$

$21 : 60 = 0.35$
